newsitem.title: FRANCE: Giscard d'Estaing calls for franc depreciation.
newsitem.headline: Giscard d'Estaing calls for franc depreciation.

text.p: France should announce plans to fix the franc against the euro at a much lower level than it is now, opening the way to a depreciation which would revive growth, former French President Valery Giscard d'Estaing said in an article published in weekly magazine l'Express.

He argued that the government should announce that the franc would be fixed at a rate of seven francs per euro -- corresponding to a more appropriate level against the dollar of 5.49 francs per dollar, compared with 5.08 francs now.
This would correspond to 3.65 francs per mark, against 3.38 today -- still within the 15 percent fluctuation bands permitted under the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), he said.

The government should announce its target exchange rate for the franc against the euro in the next few days or in any case before the end of the year to set the French currency on course towards this rate and avoid instability in the switch to the single currency in 1999, he said.

The best time, he suggested, would be just after parliament approved a deficit-cutting budget for 1997. The National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, was due to vote on the 1997 budget later on Wednesday.

Giscard said he had always believed the most important decision for France ahead of Economic and Monetary Union was to decide the rate at which the franc would be fixed irrevocably against the euro since Paris would, from 1999, never again have the option to adjust its exchange rate to boost growth.
The franc, however, was currently overvalued against the dollar and this was the main reason for weak growth and "intolerable" levels of unemployment, he said.

The overvaluation was due to a "stubborn" determination to keep the franc level-pegging with the mark, despite a sharp rise in the German currency due to the high German interest rates imposed after unification.
The franc should be brought back to the rate against the dollar seen at the start of the 1990s, in other words at 5.50 francs, he added.

France could achieve this rate by announcing its plans to fix the franc at seven francs per euro. This would provide a round number easily understood by French people, rather than the five decimal points for exchange rates foreseen under existing plans.
Based on current exchange rates against the ecu, for which the euro will be exchanged one-for-one, it would correspond to a rate of 5.49 francs per dollar.

"If the government let its intention be known to fix a parity of seven francs for one euro, corresponding to 5.50 francs per dollar, we would have within six to nine months a significant acceleration in growth," he said.
Ideally, Germany would act at the same time to modify the exchange rate of the mark against the dollar, but this seemed unlikely.
Germany did not consult its partners when it fixed the parity between the west and east German marks. "So for us, fixing our rate for entry into the euro is a national issue," Giscard said.
